title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 8
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A coffee roastery introduced a subscription service and reports that subscribers buy more coffee per year than customers who order individually. The roastery concludes that subscriptions increase consumption.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Subscribers can pause deliveries at any time.
B. Subscription coffee is delivered by post.
C. The roastery offers a discount on the first subscription order.
D. Customers who already drank a great deal of coffee were the most likely to subscribe.
E. Some subscribers also buy individually.
questions.explanation: Heavy drinkers select into subscription, so the difference may exist before any effect of the service. D would attract subscribers without explaining the difference in annual volume.

questions.prompt: A hospital charges for parking and proposes to abolish the charge, arguing that free parking will reduce the number of patients who miss appointments.
questions.question: The argument depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: A. Parking cost is among the reasons patients currently miss appointments.
B. The hospital can afford to lose the parking revenue.
C. Most patients travel to the hospital by car.
D. The car park is currently full at peak times.
E. Patients who miss an appointment are offered another within a week.
questions.explanation: Negate it: if the charge is no reason anyone misses an appointment, abolishing it cannot reduce missed appointments, and the argument collapses. A concerns affordability rather than whether the aim is achieved, and C is stronger than the argument needs - it requires only that some affected patients drive.

questions.prompt: A school district introduced free breakfast clubs and reports that attendance at the participating schools has improved. A councillor concludes that providing breakfast improves attendance.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the councillor's conclusion?
options: A. Parents report that their children enjoy the breakfasts.
B. Schools were selected for the scheme by lottery among applicants, and attendance at unsuccessful applicant schools was unchanged.
C. The breakfasts are nutritionally balanced.
D. The scheme is cheaper than employing additional attendance officers.
E. Attendance improves nationally in most years.
questions.explanation: A lottery among applicants produces a comparison group with the same motivation to apply, which is the confound that matters. E supplies a rival explanation instead.

questions.prompt: A dam has trapped sediment that formerly reached the coast, and the beaches downstream have eroded. Engineers propose releasing sediment periodically through the dam to restore the beaches.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the proposal?
options: A. How much electricity the dam generates
B. Whether the dam was built before or after the beaches began to erode
C. How many people visit the beaches each year
D. Whether other dams have been removed elsewhere
E. Whether the trapped sediment is of a grain size that will remain on the beaches rather than being carried offshore
questions.explanation: Fine sediment washes out to sea and does not build beach; the proposal only works if the material is the right size. C is already implied by the premise that trapping caused the erosion.

questions.prompt: Every model of telephone sold by the Larkhill chain that has a replaceable battery also has a headphone socket. No model with a headphone socket is waterproof. Some models sold by the chain are waterproof.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. No model with a replaceable battery is popular.
B. Every waterproof model has a sealed battery compartment.
C. Some models sold by the chain do not have a replaceable battery.
D. Most models have headphone sockets.
E. Waterproof models cost more than others.
questions.explanation: Waterproof models exist; waterproof implies no headphone socket, and replaceable battery implies a socket, so waterproof models cannot have replaceable batteries. C sounds plausible physically but does not follow from the statements.

questions.prompt: A manufacturer extended its product warranty from two years to five and reports that warranty claims in the third year of ownership are rare. It concludes that its products are more reliable than competitors' products, which are warranted for two years.
questions.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. ignores the cost of honouring warranty claims
B. assumes that claims made under a warranty measure the rate at which products fail
C. relies on data from a single year
D. does not distinguish between models
E. overlooks the possibility that customers prefer longer warranties
questions.explanation: Owners of a failed product may repair it, replace it, or not bother claiming; claim rates track claiming behaviour as much as failure, and competitors' products are not covered in year three at all, so no comparison is available.

questions.prompt: A museum replaced its incandescent gallery lighting with LEDs and reports that visitor numbers rose the following year. The director attributes the rise to the improved appearance of the galleries.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the director's attribution?
options: A. LEDs consume less electricity than incandescent lamps.
B. Some visitors say the new lighting is too bright.
C. The lighting was installed over several months.
D. Other museums in the city also replaced their lighting.
E. The museum's most popular touring exhibition of the decade ran for eight months of that year.
questions.explanation: A major touring exhibition explains the rise without reference to the lighting. C would weaken the mechanism slightly; A is irrelevant to attendance.

questions.prompt: A recruitment consultancy found that job advertisements listing a salary range attract more applicants than those that do not, and advises all its clients to list salary ranges in order to increase the number of applicants they receive.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the advice as a general recommendation?
options: A. For roles where the offered pay is below the market rate, listing the range reduces applications sharply.
B. Some applicants apply to many positions.
C. Advertisements are usually written by hiring managers.
D. Applicant numbers vary by season.
E. Listing a range is required by law in some jurisdictions.
questions.explanation: The advice is general; a category in which the effect reverses shows the recommendation cannot be applied without regard to the pay on offer.

questions.prompt: A bicycle-sharing scheme moves bicycles overnight from stations where they accumulate to stations where they run short. The operator reports that since it began this rebalancing, the number of trips has risen, and concludes that rebalancing has increased use.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the conclusion?
options: A. The scheme has added new stations in the same period.
B. Rebalancing is carried out by van.
C. On nights when rebalancing was suspended for operational reasons, the following day's trips fell sharply at exactly the stations that would have been restocked.
D. Members can see station occupancy on a mobile application.
E. Trips are counted electronically at each docking point.
questions.explanation: Suspension nights supply a within-scheme comparison isolating the effect at the affected stations. A introduces a rival explanation for the overall rise.

questions.prompt: A wine producer notes that its wines have won more medals at international competitions since it began ageing them in new oak barrels, and concludes that new oak improves its wine.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. New barrels are considerably more expensive than used ones.
B. Some producers use oak chips rather than barrels.
C. The producer entered more competitions than before.

D. Competition judges taste young wines, in which the flavours contributed by new oak are most prominent, and the same wines have been rated less favourably by critics assessing them after several years in bottle.
E. Medals are awarded in several categories.
questions.explanation: It offers a reason why medals rose without the wine being better — the judging conditions favour the new characteristic — and adds contrary evidence from a different assessment. D would explain more medals but not a higher rate of success.

questions.prompt: Supporters of a timber certification scheme argue that it reduces deforestation, since certified forests are logged at lower intensity than uncertified ones. Critics reply that certification is granted mainly to forests that were already well managed.
questions.question: The critics' reply is best described as
options: A. denying that certified forests are logged at lower intensity
B. arguing that the observed difference may reflect which forests enter the scheme rather than an effect of the scheme
C. questioning whether deforestation can be measured
D. objecting to the cost of certification
E. proposing that certification be made compulsory
questions.explanation: A selection argument: the scheme may be labelling good practice rather than producing it. The critics accept the intensity difference and dispute its cause.

questions.passageText:
Inventory is money sitting still. A firm that holds three months of components has paid for them, is storing them, and risks their becoming obsolete; a firm that holds three days has released that capital for other uses. The logic drove four decades of reduction in industrial stock levels, and the gains were real.

What the logic omits is that inventory is also insurance. A buffer absorbs variation in supply and demand, and removing it transfers that variation directly into production. The transfer is invisible while conditions are stable, which is precisely when the buffer looks most wasteful, so the incentive to cut runs strongest at the moment the protection is least obviously needed.

The exposure is worsened by a feature of modern supply chains that individual firms cannot see. Each firm knows its own suppliers; few know their suppliers' suppliers. Concentration at a lower tier — a single plant making a specialised component for the whole industry — is invisible from the top, so a network that appears diversified may share a single point of failure. Firms that believed they had three sources of a part have discovered that all three bought from the same works.

The conclusion is not that lean methods were a mistake. It is that the calculation was performed with one term missing. The cost of holding stock is measurable and appears in the accounts every month; the cost of not holding it appears rarely, falls partly on customers and other firms, and is therefore systematically underweighted by exactly the parties who decide.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the incentive to reduce inventory is strongest when
options: A. demand is growing rapidly
B. suppliers are concentrated in one region
C. conditions are stable, which is when the buffer looks most wasteful
D. capital is expensive to raise
E. components are at risk of becoming obsolete
questions.explanation: The second paragraph makes exactly this point: the transfer of variation into production is invisible while conditions are stable, so pressure to cut peaks when protection seems least necessary.

options: A. concentration at a lower tier of the chain is invisible from the top
B. its suppliers conceal their production volumes
C. it has not audited its own inventory records
D. diversification is measured by value rather than by volume

options: A. it was based on faulty accounting data
B. it applied only to manufacturing firms
C. it underestimated the cost of warehousing
D. it omitted a term whose cost falls partly on parties other than the decision-maker

questions.passageText:
Galaxies rotate too quickly. Stars far from the centre of a spiral galaxy move at speeds that the gravitational pull of the visible matter cannot explain; on the visible mass alone, such galaxies should fly apart. Two families of response exist, and the contest between them is a useful example of how a theory earns preference.

The first supposes additional matter that does not emit light. Dark matter accounts for the rotation curves, and — more importantly — for phenomena it was not devised to explain: the bending of light around clusters, the pattern of fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background, and the rate at which structure formed in the early universe. Its weakness is direct detection. Decades of increasingly sensitive experiments have not identified a particle.

The second modifies gravity itself. Modified Newtonian dynamics reproduces galaxy rotation curves with a single adjustment and does so with striking economy, predicting a regularity in the relation between visible mass and rotation speed that dark matter models must fit rather than derive. Its difficulty is scale: the modification that works for individual galaxies does not account for clusters without additional unseen mass, and it has no comparable account of the microwave background.

The present position is asymmetric rather than settled. Dark matter explains more phenomena but has not been found; modified gravity explains one class of phenomenon more elegantly but does not extend. What would change the picture is not another rotation curve, which both accommodate, but a detection, or a system in which the two make opposite predictions.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that the principal strength of the dark matter explanation is that it
options: A. has been confirmed by direct detection of a particle
B. requires no modification of existing physical law
C. is simpler than the alternative
D. predicts the relation between visible mass and rotation speed
E. accounts for phenomena it was not devised to explain
questions.explanation: Light bending around clusters, the microwave background and early structure formation are named as phenomena beyond the rotation curves it was introduced for. E describes the strength of the rival.

questions.passageTitle: Roads and the Traffic That Fills Them
questions.passageText:
Widening a congested road reliably reduces congestion for a period, after which traffic returns to something near its former level. The observation is old, has been confirmed across many countries, and is still widely treated as a surprise.

The mechanism is not mysterious. Congestion is a price paid in time, and travel demand responds to it like any other price. When capacity rises, the time cost falls, and journeys that were not worth making at the old cost become worth making. Some are new trips; some are existing trips shifted from other routes, other times of day, or other modes; over longer periods, some result from decisions about where to live and where to locate a business, which is why the full effect takes years to appear and is missed by short evaluations.

Two misreadings follow. The first treats induced demand as showing that road building is futile. It is not: the additional journeys are journeys people wanted to make, and their value is a benefit even though it does not appear as a reduction in travel time. The second treats it as an argument for doing nothing, which ignores that the same logic applies to any capacity — a new railway line fills up too.

The practical implication is about measurement rather than construction. A scheme justified by forecast time savings that will be eroded by the traffic it induces has been justified on the wrong ground, and the honest case for it must rest on the value of the extra access it creates.
questions.prompt: The passage explains the return of congestion after a road is widened chiefly by
options: A. population growth in the surrounding area
B. the deterioration of the new road surface
C. the response of travel demand to a fall in the time cost of a journey
D. the failure of drivers to use alternative routes
E. errors in the original traffic forecasts
questions.explanation: Congestion is treated as a price paid in time, and demand responds to it as to any price.

options: A. Some of the response comes through decisions about where to live and locate a business.
B. Construction is completed in stages.

options: A. road building should generally be avoided
B. capacity should be added to railways instead
C. congestion charging is the only effective remedy
D. traffic forecasts should be produced more frequently
E. schemes should be justified by the value of the access they create rather than by forecast time savings

questions.passageText:
Linear perspective — the geometric construction by which parallel lines converge on a vanishing point — was formalised in Florence in the early fifteenth century. It is often described as the discovery of how to represent the world correctly, and that description contains an assumption worth examining.

The construction is genuinely a discovery in one sense. It is a correct solution to a stated problem: how to project a three-dimensional scene onto a plane as it would appear from one fixed point, with one eye, at one moment. Painters who applied it could produce images that a viewer standing in the right place found convincing, and the technique spread quickly because the effect was unmistakable.

The assumption is that this is what a picture is for. The conditions the construction requires — a single eye, a fixed position, an instant — are not the conditions under which people see. Traditions that arranged figures by importance rather than distance, or showed several moments in one frame, were not failing at perspective; they were solving a different problem, and one of their solutions preserved information that perspective discards.

Later European painting itself moved away from strict construction, not through incompetence but because artists found the fixed viewpoint a constraint on what they wanted to say. The useful formulation is that perspective is one representational technology among several, unusually powerful for a particular purpose, and that calling it correctness mistakes a choice of problem for a standard of accuracy.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that linear perspective solves the problem of representing a scene
options: A. as it appears to two eyes in motion
B. as it is understood rather than seen
C. with figures arranged according to their importance
D. as it would appear from one fixed point, with one eye, at one moment
E. without reference to the position of the viewer
questions.explanation: The stated conditions of the construction, which the passage then observes are not the conditions of ordinary seeing.

When capacity rises, the time cost falls, and journeys that were not worth making at the old cost become worth making. Some are new trips; some are existing trips shifted from other routes, other times of day, or other modes; over longer periods, some result from decisions about where to live and where to locate a business, which is why the full effect takes years to appear and is missed by short evaluations.

Two misreadings follow. The first treats induced demand as showing that road building is futile. It is not: the additional journeys are journeys people wanted to make, and their value is a benefit even though it does not appear as a reduction in travel time. The second treats it as an argument for doing nothing, which ignores that the same logic applies to any capacity — a new railway line fills up too.

The practical implication is about measurement rather than construction. A scheme justified by forecast time savings that will be eroded by the traffic it induces has been justified on the wrong ground, and the honest case for it must rest on the value of the extra access it creates.

readingPassages.title: Learning to Paint Depth
readingPassages.text:
Linear perspective — the geometric construction by which parallel lines converge on a vanishing point — was formalised in Florence in the early fifteenth century. It is often described as the discovery of how to represent the world correctly, and that description contains an assumption worth examining.

The construction is genuinely a discovery in one sense. It is a correct solution to a stated problem: how to project a three-dimensional scene onto a plane as it would appear from one fixed point, with one eye, at one moment. Painters who applied it could produce images that a viewer standing in the right place found convincing, and the technique spread quickly because the effect was unmistakable.

The assumption is that this is what a picture is for. The conditions the construction requires — a single eye, a fixed position, an instant — are not the conditions under which people see. Traditions that arranged figures by importance rather than distance, or showed several moments in one frame, were not failing at perspective; they were solving a different problem, and one of their solutions preserved information that perspective discards.

Later European painting itself moved away from strict construction, not through incompetence but because artists found the fixed viewpoint a constraint on what they wanted to say. The useful formulation is that perspective is one representational technology among several, unusually powerful for a particular purpose, and that calling it correctness mistakes a choice of problem for a standard of accuracy.
